narrativeReportMd:
# DeviceRequest R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking changes were found. The resource identity is stable, but several local DeviceRequest elements were removed, renamed, merged, or retyped. The most important hard break is that mandatory R4 `code[x]` became mandatory R6 `product[x]`; every unconverted R4 DeviceRequest is expected to fail R6 validation because the required choice element name changed.

## Scope
The analysis used the local R4 and R6 core packages, package indexes, package metadata, DeviceRequest StructureDefinitions, CodeableReference, and request status/intent terminology resources. Inherited base-resource changes are excluded from findings and listed out of scope.

## Main migration themes
DeviceRequest adopts R6 request-pattern naming and CodeableReference modeling: `priorRequest` becomes `replaces`, `code[x]` becomes `product[x]`, `performer` changes from Reference to CodeableReference, `performerType` is removed, and `reasonCode`/`reasonReference` merge into `reason`. R6 also adds new semantic capacity (`doNotPerform`, quantity/location, PRN fields) that cannot be represented in base R4 without extensions or policy. Required request status/intent bindings add R6-only codes.

## Highest-impact findings
The high-impact local issues are the mandatory `code[x]` to `product[x]` replacement, the `performer` datatype replacement, the reason merge, the safety-critical `doNotPerform` modifier, and R6-only required intent/status codes.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for removed protocol-definition links, non-DeviceRequest `priorRequest` targets, `productCanonical`, negative requests using `doNotPerform`, combined CodeableReference reasons/performers, and down-mapping R6-only status/intent codes.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Many structural breaks could have been softened with deprecated aliases or cross-version extensions, but the R6 model is generally more explicit and coherent. The tradeoff is that implementers need deliberate transforms rather than relying on permissive parsing.

## Follow-up analysis
Separate reports should cover CodeableReference, Resource/DomainResource inherited changes, and shared request terminology/ConceptMaps so reducers can separate local DeviceRequest breaks from cross-artifact vocabulary and base-model changes.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: DeviceRequest has material local R4-to-R6 breaks: mandatory `code[x]` is now `product[x]`, several optional elements were removed/merged into CodeableReference forms, and R6 adds modifier/terminology semantics that older systems cannot safely ignore. The largest uncertainty is official cross-version mapping guidance for removed fields and new request-status/intent codes.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should be transform-driven, not parser-tolerant. Rename mandatory product fields, wrap Reference values in CodeableReference where required, merge/split reason and performer role information carefully, preserve removed protocol links with an agreed extension if needed, and define policy for R6-only negative requests, quantity/location/PRN details, requester targets, and request status/intent codes.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for local structural deltas because both assigned StructureDefinitions and package indexes were available and directly compared. Confidence is medium for the precise business mapping of some changes because official diffs, narrative migration notes, and cross-version ConceptMaps were not supplied. Example-bound terminology comparisons are lower risk because their binding strength is not required.

findings.title: Protocol-definition links instantiatesCanonical and instantiatesUri were removed from DeviceRequest

oldState.summary: R4 allowed zero or more canonical links to ActivityDefinition/PlanDefinition and zero or more external URI links.

semanticText.short: Instantiates FHIR protocol or definition / Instantiates external protocol or definition
semanticText.definition: URLs pointing to FHIR-defined or externally maintained protocols, guidelines, ordersets or other definitions adhered to by the DeviceRequest.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 instances could explicitly say that the device request followed a FHIR ActivityDefinition/PlanDefinition or an external protocol URI.

newState.summary: No local R6 DeviceRequest element carries this protocol-definition linkage.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 DeviceRequest snapshot has no `instantiatesCanonical` or `instantiatesUri` element.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 instance containing either removed property will fail strict R6 parsing/validation because the elements are no longer part of the resource. The impact is high for workflows that use DeviceRequest to preserve guideline, order-set, or protocol provenance, even though prevalence is unknown.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Losing the link to the ordering protocol can affect auditability, decision-support traceability, and payer or operational review.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal of aligning DeviceRequest with the R6 request model is reasonable, but the supplied R6 StructureDefinition shows no native replacement for these optional protocol-definition links. Keeping them as deprecated optional elements would have preserved R4-valid instances and protocol provenance while still allowing R6 guidance to prefer another pattern. With only modest long-term cost, full removal from the base resource looks probably avoidable.
justification.inferredGoal: Align DeviceRequest with the R6 request model by removing local protocol-instantiation fields.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the optional R4 instantiatesCanonical and instantiatesUri elements as deprecated while documenting any preferred R6 pattern.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep `DeviceRequest.instantiatesCanonical` and `DeviceRequest.instantiatesUri` in R6 as deprecated optional elements, with text directing new implementations to the preferred R6 mechanism if one exists. That is a real base-design alternative, unlike migration-time extension preservation, because unconverted R4 instances would remain valid.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Some legacy model clutter and possible duplicate provenance paths, but low validation ambiguity because the fields are optional and distinct.

evidence.detail: R4 defines instantiatesCanonical as 0..* canonical targeting ActivityDefinition and PlanDefinition.
evidence.quote: The URL pointing to a FHIR-defined protocol, guideline, orderset or other definition...

evidence.detail: R4 defines instantiatesUri as 0..* uri for external protocols or definitions.
evidence.quote: The URL pointing to an externally maintained protocol, guideline, orderset or other definition...

evidence.detail: R6 has no DeviceRequest.instantiatesCanonical or DeviceRequest.instantiatesUri element.

examples.examplesMd: The fragments are illustrative and focus on the changed fields; a production transform should use an agreed cross-version extension or other policy for preserving removed protocol links.

findings.narrativeMd: `DeviceRequest.instantiatesCanonical` and `DeviceRequest.instantiatesUri` disappeared locally from DeviceRequest. This is a direct wire-format break for R4 instances that used the fields, and it can also be a semantic loss because there is no obvious native R6 field on DeviceRequest for the same protocol-definition link.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances containing either property are old-valid/new-invalid under strict R6 validation. R6-to-R4 is not the problem here because R6 no longer has the data; the migration risk is preserving R4 information that R6 cannot natively carry.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory use of both fields before conversion. If the information must be retained, define a cross-version extension or a companion Provenance/metadata policy, and test that validators do not silently drop summary-level protocol links.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because both elements were optional, a less disruptive path was available: keep them as deprecated optional elements and document the preferred R6 mechanism. Removal simplifies the base resource but forces senders and converters to decide where to store potentially important protocol provenance.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 allowed DeviceRequest instances to carry protocol, guideline, order-set, or definition links through `instantiatesCanonical` and `instantiatesUri`; R6 removes both without a native same-resource replacement. This is optional and likely not universally used, but when it is used the migration is lossy or extension-dependent rather than a simple rename. Because these fields were optional and summary-level, retaining them as deprecated compatibility fields looks like a relatively low-cost base design that would preserve existing instances while R6 clarified preferred workflow modeling.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.instantiatesCanonical` is 0..* canonical(ActivityDefinition|PlanDefinition).
R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.instantiatesUri` is 0..* uri for external protocols or definitions.
R6 StructureDefinition: no `DeviceRequest.instantiatesCanonical` or `DeviceRequest.instantiatesUri` element is present.
Quick public check found an HL7 QI-Core DeviceRequest profile, suggesting artifact-level implementation relevance, but no path-specific evidence for these fields.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use softens the presumption of broad deployed impact, so the judgment is not based on breakage alone. The remaining concern is the low-cost deprecated-field alternative and potential audit/decision-support traceability loss for implementations that did use these optional links.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 instances containing either removed property are not valid against the R6 DeviceRequest shape, and preserving the data requires an extension or external policy.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could plausibly have retained both optional elements as deprecated while documenting a preferred R6 pattern. The tradeoff is some legacy surface area and possible duplicate provenance concepts, but the fields are optional, distinct, and not in conflict with the new R6 elements.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment: the hard break and less-breaking option are real, but the existing high-impact framing should be tempered by FMM 1 and unknown path-specific prevalence.

findings.title: priorRequest was removed and a narrower replaces element was added

semanticText.definition: The request takes the place of the referenced completed or terminated request(s).

oldState.narrativeMd: `priorRequest` could point to any Resource and was mapped to the workflow `Request.replaces` concept.

semanticText.definition: The request takes the place of the referenced completed or terminated request(s).

newState.narrativeMd: `replaces` carries the same high-level replacement meaning but uses a new element name and only allows DeviceRequest targets.

facts.note: The effective allowed reference target is narrowed.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements have the same short/definition and the R4 element maps to workflow `Request.replaces`; R6 uses that workflow name as the local path. Path identity still changed, so tools must transform the property name.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 JSON using `priorRequest` will not validate as R6. Even after renaming, references to resources other than DeviceRequest become invalid because R6 narrows the target profile. R6 `replaces` values can be represented in R4 by transforming the path back to `priorRequest` because R4 allowed any Resource target.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Replacement chains affect fulfillment, duplicate-order suppression, and audit history; broken links may lead systems to treat superseded requests as independent.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is coherent: use the common `replaces` request-pattern name and restrict replacement chains to DeviceRequest predecessors. A less-breaking design could have retained the old `priorRequest` name, because living with a nonoptimal R4 name is a legitimate compatibility strategy. However, preserving all R4-valid instances would also preserve broad `Reference(Resource)` targets or duplicate the relationship under two names, which carries real validation and interoperability cost.
justification.inferredGoal: Use the common Request.replaces naming and restrict replacement links to same-resource DeviceRequest predecessors.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep priorRequest as a deprecated alias and/or temporarily allow broader Resource targets while adding replaces.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The strongest alternative would keep `priorRequest` as an optional deprecated alias for `replaces`, perhaps with guidance that only DeviceRequest targets are preferred in R6. This would cover common same-resource replacement cases but would either reject old cross-resource targets or keep looser target validation than the R6 design intends, so the alternative is only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Aliases and broad targets preserve more R4 data but create duplicate same-resource relationship names and weaken R6 same-resource replacement validation.

evidence.detail: R4 priorRequest is Reference(Resource), 0..*, with definition "The request takes the place...".
R6 replaces is Reference(DeviceRequest), 0..*, with the same definition.
The R4 workflow mapping is Request.replaces, supporting the semantic match.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is only valid when the prior request is actually a DeviceRequest. Other target types need manual review or an extension.

findings.narrativeMd: `priorRequest` is not just a spelling change: the R6 element is named `replaces` and narrows references to DeviceRequest. Existing R4 data with replacement links will be rejected until the field is renamed, and some previously legal cross-resource references cannot be represented as R6 `replaces`.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `priorRequest` are old-valid/new-invalid. A transformed R4 `priorRequest` that points to a non-DeviceRequest resource remains invalid in R6 because of target-profile validation. R6-to-R4 conversion is structurally possible by using `priorRequest`, but round-trip identity still depends on converter rules.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `priorRequest` to `replaces` only for references that resolve to DeviceRequest or are known to identify DeviceRequest. Flag all other targets for human review and preserve them in an extension or external relationship table if they matter.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The more precise R6 model is understandable, but a compatibility alias or wider target during transition would have avoided rejecting existing replacement links. The cost of compatibility would be looser validation and duplicate relationship names.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `priorRequest` becomes `replaces`, and the target narrows from any Resource to DeviceRequest. An R4 sender must transform the property name, and old cross-resource replacement links need policy. The R6 goal is understandable: align with the common request relationship name and constrain replacement chains to the same request resource. A compatibility alias would help, but it would leave duplicate relationship names and either keep broad targets or create non-obvious rejection rules.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.priorRequest` is 0..* Reference(Resource) with replacement semantics.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.replaces` is 0..* Reference(DeviceRequest) with the same replacement definition.
R4 workflow mapping for `priorRequest` is `Request.replaces`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use lowers the stability burden. Replacement links can matter for audit and duplicate-order suppression, but there is no supplied or quickly found evidence that broad cross-resource `priorRequest` use is common enough to override the R6 modeling rationale.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: the old property name is rejected in R6, and even after renaming, non-DeviceRequest targets no longer fit the R6 target profile.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. A deprecated `priorRequest` alias could preserve many same-resource R4 instances, but it would duplicate `replaces`; preserving all old instances would also weaken the R6 target restriction to DeviceRequest.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment: the report correctly identifies the hard break and partial alternative, but I judge the break proportionate under low FMM because the alternative has real model and validation costs.

findings.title: Mandatory code[x] was replaced by mandatory product[x] and gained canonical(DeviceDefinition)

oldState.summary: R4 required code[x] 1..1 with Reference(Device) or CodeableConcept.

binding.description: Codes for devices that can be requested.

semanticText.definition: The details of the device to be used.

oldState.narrativeMd: Every valid R4 DeviceRequest must carry `codeCodeableConcept` or `codeReference`.

newState.summary: R6 requires product[x] 1..1 with CodeableConcept, Reference(Device), or canonical(DeviceDefinition).

binding.description: Codes for devices that can be requested.

semanticText.definition: The details of the device to be used.

newState.narrativeMd: The same mandatory concept is now serialized under `productCodeableConcept`, `productReference`, or `productCanonical`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The elements have the same short, definition, cardinality, and binding name, but the path and choice-element JSON property names changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is the highest-prevalence structural break because `code[x]` is mandatory in R4. Strict R6 parsers will reject the R4 choice property name. R6 also adds `productCanonical` targeting DeviceDefinition, which has no R4 `code[x]` equivalent.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The requested device is the core clinical/business payload; losing or failing to transform it makes the order unusable.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying that the ordered item is a product/device and allowing DeviceDefinition canonicals are reasonable R6 goals. The breaking rename is harder to justify because `code[x]` is mandatory in R4, so every unconverted valid R4 DeviceRequest depends on that name. Retaining the old choice name while broadening the type set would preserve essentially all R4 instances and still support the key new DeviceDefinition use case with only a moderate naming tradeoff.
justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the ordered item is the product/device rather than a generic code and allow references to DeviceDefinition.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep required code[x] and add canonical(DeviceDefinition) as an additional choice type with clearer definitions and profile guidance.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would leave `DeviceRequest.code[x]` in place, update its definition to describe the requested product/device more clearly, and add `canonical(DeviceDefinition)` to the existing CodeableConcept and Reference(Device) choices. This avoids duplicate same-resource fields and makes the cost mainly cosmetic: implementers would live with the older `code` name for one more release.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The nonoptimal `code` name would persist and `codeCanonical` is less intuitive than `productCanonical`, but the substantive R6 product/catalog goal would be met without invalidating R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 code[x] is mandatory 1..1 and supports Reference(Device) or CodeableConcept.
evidence.quote: The details of the device to be used.

evidence.detail: R6 product[x] is mandatory 1..1 and supports CodeableConcept, Reference(Device), or canonical(DeviceDefinition).
The R6 example value set includes ISO 11073 device type codes and SNOMED filters; binding remains example, so it is not a required-code validation break.

examples.examplesMd: R4 `codeCodeableConcept` maps mechanically to R6 `productCodeableConcept`, and R4 `codeReference` maps to R6 `productReference`. R6 `productCanonical` requires a policy for R4 representation.

findings.narrativeMd: The requested device element moved from `code[x]` to `product[x]`. Since this element is required, untransformed R4 instances are expected to fail R6 validation. Generated models, serializers, search/extraction code, and FHIRPath expressions that mention `codeCodeableConcept` or `codeReference` must be updated to the `product...` choice names.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-valid DeviceRequest instances are new-invalid until the choice property is renamed. R6 `productCodeableConcept` and `productReference` can be converted back to R4 `code[x]`, but R6 `productCanonical` cannot be represented natively in R4 without resolving or extension-preserving the DeviceDefinition canonical.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Apply a deterministic field rename for CodeableConcept and Device reference cases. For `productCanonical`, decide whether to resolve to a Device, translate to a code, or preserve the canonical in an extension. Test all three R6 product choice types and verify downstream code that treats the requested device as mandatory.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The clearer R6 name and DeviceDefinition support have clear modeling value. The backward-compatible alternative would have been to add canonical support or a product alias while retaining `code[x]`; that would have reduced migration failures at the cost of duplicated semantics in the resource.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `code[x]` is the required R4 element carrying the requested device, and R6 changes the required wire name to `product[x]` while adding `productCanonical`. Because every valid R4 DeviceRequest has the old choice name, this is a high-certainty parser, validator, codegen, and mapper break on the central payload. The substantive R6 improvement, including DeviceDefinition canonical support, could mostly have been achieved by keeping the R4 choice name and widening its allowed types.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.code[x]` is 1..1 and allows Reference(Device) or CodeableConcept.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.product[x]` is 1..1 and allows CodeableConcept, Reference(Device), or canonical(DeviceDefinition).
R4 and R6 definitions both describe the details of the device to be used.
HL7 QI-Core has DeviceRequest profiles, supporting artifact-level implementation relevance for central request content.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Although supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use weakens stability expectations, this path is mandatory and central to the resource. Low FMM does not erase the fact that generated APIs and all valid R4 instances depend on the old choice name.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: unconverted R4 `codeCodeableConcept` or `codeReference` properties do not satisfy the required R6 `product[x]` element; R6 `productCanonical` also has no native R4 equivalent.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained required `code[x]`, clarified its wording as the requested product/device, and added canonical(DeviceDefinition) as another choice. The tradeoff is living with the less precise `code` name and a less elegant `codeCanonical` property, but it avoids invalidating all R4 instances.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing high-impact and less-breaking-alternative judgment: this is a central mandatory rename with a plausible less-breaking base design.

findings.title: performer changed at the same path from Reference to CodeableReference

oldState.summary: R4 performer was 0..1 Reference to practitioner, organization, team, service, patient, device, or related person.

semanticText.definition: The desired performer for doing the diagnostic testing.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 serialized the performer directly as a Reference object such as `"performer": {"reference": "Practitioner/1"}`.

newState.summary: R6 performer is 0..1 CodeableReference with the same reference target profiles.

semanticText.definition: The desired individual or entity to provide the device to the subject of the request (e.g., patient, location).

newState.narrativeMd: R6 wraps the reference under CodeableReference, so the equivalent reference is `"performer": {"reference": {"reference": "Practitioner/1"}}`; it may also carry a `concept`.

facts.note: Target resources are preserved, but nested under CodeableReference.reference.

facts.oldValue: The desired performer for doing the diagnostic testing.
facts.newValue: The desired individual or entity to provide the device to the subject of the request (e.g., patient, location).

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a same-path datatype replacement with incompatible JSON shape. A direct R4 Reference object under `performer` is not a valid R6 CodeableReference. Generated classes also change from a Reference property to a CodeableReference property.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The desired performer can affect routing and fulfillment responsibility; losing it can misdirect work.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Using CodeableReference is a reasonable R6 modeling goal because it lets a performer be identified by concept, reference, or both. A less-breaking design exists for common cases: keep the R4 `performer` Reference and continue using a separate coded role element. The tradeoff is material because it fails the unified representation goal and can obscure whether a code and reference are intended as one paired performer.
justification.inferredGoal: Allow performer to be specified either as a concrete actor reference or as a coded class of performer.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep performer as Reference and retain or add a separate coded performer-role field instead of replacing the same path with CodeableReference.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best compatibility design would keep `performer` as a direct Reference and carry coded performer classes in `performerType` or another optional coded field. That preserves R4 wire format for reference performers, but it is incomplete for R6 because it lacks the single CodeableReference container and requires rules to keep split fields consistent.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: This preserves R4 reference-only performers but keeps split actor/role modeling and does not fully support CodeableReference concept-reference pairing.

evidence.detail: R4 performer type is Reference with eight target profiles.
R6 performer type is CodeableReference with the same target profiles.
CodeableReference.reference is a child Reference element, not the same JSON shape as Reference itself.

examples.examplesMd: The only shown change is the CodeableReference wrapper; product renaming is included so the example is R6-shaped.

findings.narrativeMd: `DeviceRequest.performer` kept its path but changed datatype. This is easy to miss because the element name did not change; nevertheless the serialized JSON shape and generated property type changed materially.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with a direct Reference in `performer` is old-valid/new-invalid. R6 instances with `performer.reference` can be downgraded to R4 `performer`; R6 instances with only `performer.concept` need mapping to R4 `performerType` or an extension, and instances with both concept and reference need careful round-trip handling.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Wrap R4 performer references as `CodeableReference.reference`. Update generated clients, FHIRPath expressions, and business rules that assumed `performer.reference` was a primitive string on the performer object. Include tests for reference-only, concept-only, and combined CodeableReference cases.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change likely reflects a broader R6 preference for CodeableReference. Keeping the same path while changing datatype maximizes conceptual continuity but minimizes wire compatibility; adding a new coded element would have been less disruptive.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `performer` keeps its path but changes from a direct Reference to CodeableReference, so the JSON shape and generated type change even for the same target resources. R4 references can usually be wrapped mechanically in `performer.reference`. R6 also gains concept-only or concept-plus-reference performer representation, and keeping the old Reference model would not meet that unified modeling goal without retaining split fields and conflict rules.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.performer` is 0..1 Reference to practitioner, organization, care team, service, patient, device, or related person targets.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.performer` is 0..1 CodeableReference with the same reference target profiles.
R6 CodeableReference represents references under a child `reference`, not as a direct Reference object.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use softens the stability concern. Performer is operationally relevant for fulfillment routing, but the common R4 reference-only case has a straightforward transform.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: the same path now has an incompatible datatype and JSON shape, so generated models, FHIRPath, serializers, and business logic that expected a direct Reference must change.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. Keeping `performer` as Reference and carrying coded performer class elsewhere would preserve old reference-only instances, but it would not support the R6 single CodeableReference container or paired concept/reference semantics.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment: the break is real, but I treat it as proportionate because the R6 CodeableReference goal has material value and the alternative is incomplete.

findings.title: performerType was removed and its role-concept content moves into performer.concept

oldState.summary: R4 performerType was 0..1 CodeableConcept with an example participant-role binding.

binding.description: Indicates specific responsibility of an individual within the care team.

semanticText.definition: Desired type of performer for doing the diagnostic testing.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 had a separate coded role/class field in addition to the concrete performer Reference.

newState.summary: R6 has no performerType element; coded performer information is represented through CodeableReference.concept on performer.
newState.narrativeMd: A coded performer role must be embedded in `performer.concept`, sharing the single `performer` element with any performer reference.

facts.note: Inferred from R6 performer CodeableReference and preserved actor semantics.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: R6 CodeableReference can carry a coded concept at `performer.concept`, but the R6 StructureDefinition does not explicitly name `performerType` as the predecessor.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `performerType` will fail strict R6 validation unless converted. Most content can be moved into `performer.concept`, but code that expected a separate performer-role property must change.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Performer role can drive routing and assignment; losing it can reduce fulfillment accuracy.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Consolidating performer role and performer reference into a CodeableReference is coherent with the R6 performer design. Keeping `performerType` would have preserved R4 instances, but it would leave two same-resource ways to express the same performer concept and could produce conflicting or permanently duplicated representations. Those material tradeoffs make the alternative partial rather than a clean Yes.
justification.inferredGoal: Consolidate performer class and performer reference using CodeableReference.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain performerType as a deprecated compatibility alias to performer.concept.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking R6 base could keep `performerType` as optional and deprecated, define it as an alias for `performer.concept`, and warn when both are populated inconsistently. This covers R4 data well, but it undermines the consolidation goal and risks deprecated role fields accumulating indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old coded-role data but creates duplicate role representations and requires conflict rules when both performerType and performer.concept are present.

evidence.detail: R4 defines performerType as 0..1 CodeableConcept with participant-role example binding.
R6 has no DeviceRequest.performerType element.
CodeableReference.concept is a 0..1 CodeableConcept child that can carry a class-level concept.

examples.examplesMd: When R4 has both `performerType` and `performer`, R6 can usually carry both in one CodeableReference with `concept` and `reference`, but converters should verify that this combined representation is acceptable for their profiles.

findings.narrativeMd: `performerType` was removed as a standalone element. Although R6 CodeableReference provides a likely destination for the coded performer class, this is still a hard wire-format break for R4 instances and a generated-model break for applications.

This breaks R4 instances that used the separate field, especially generated models and mappers, but the migration is usually direct unless old data also has a performer reference whose association needs to be preserved. findings.title: reasonCode and reasonReference were merged into reason CodeableReference

oldState.summary: R4 had separate 0..* reasonCode CodeableConcept and 0..* reasonReference Reference arrays.

binding.description: Diagnosis or problem codes justifying the reason for requesting the device.

semanticText.short: Coded Reason for request / Linked Reason for request
semanticText.definition: Reason or justification for the use of this device.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 encoded coded and referenced reasons in two independent arrays.

newState.summary: R6 has one 0..* reason CodeableReference array with the same reference target profiles and condition-code example binding.

binding.description: Diagnosis or problem codes justifying the reason for requesting the device.

semanticText.definition: Reason or justification for the use of this device.
semanticText.comment: When doNotPerform is true, this is the reason for requesting not to provide the device.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 represents coded and referenced reasons as entries in a single CodeableReference array.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 element preserves the old definition, summary flag, reference target set, and example binding while changing the representation to CodeableReference.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances with either `reasonCode` or `reasonReference` will not validate as R6 until transformed. R6 entries can carry a concept and a reference together; R4 can split them into two arrays but cannot preserve the fact that a specific concept and reference were paired in the same CodeableReference without extension support.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Reason information can explain medical necessity or, with doNotPerform, why a device must not be used.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of unifying coded and linked reasons under CodeableReference is reasonable and adds expressive value, including preserving a code/reference pair as one reason. Retaining the old arrays would preserve R4 instances, but it would also create duplicate same-resource representations for reasons and weaken the single-container model. Because the less-breaking design is useful but materially incomplete and ambiguous, the break is probably justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Unify coded and referenced reasons under CodeableReference and align with R6 request patterns.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep reasonCode and reasonReference as deprecated aliases while adding reason CodeableReference.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best alternative would keep `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` as optional deprecated aliases for `reason[].concept` and `reason[].reference`. This avoids immediate R4 validation failures, but R6 instances with both concept and reference in one CodeableReference cannot be represented cleanly in the old split arrays without losing the pairing or adding extra metadata.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves common R4 reason data but introduces competing representations and conflict or round-trip ambiguity, especially for paired concept-plus-reference reasons.

evidence.detail: R4 reasonCode is 0..* CodeableConcept with condition-code example binding.
R4 reasonReference is 0..* Reference to Condition, Observation, DiagnosticReport, or DocumentReference.
R6 reason is 0..* CodeableReference with the same reference targets and example binding.
R6 adds doNotPerform-related semantics to reason.
evidence.quote: When doNotPerform is true, this is the reason for requesting not to provide the device.

examples.examplesMd: Splitting an R6 CodeableReference into R4 arrays may lose pairing if both `concept` and `reference` are populated on the same R6 reason.

findings.narrativeMd: `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` became a single `reason` CodeableReference. This is a local element identity and representation change, not just a terminology update. It affects validation, generated code, FHIRPath, and any business logic that separately iterated coded versus linked reasons.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `reasonCode` or `reasonReference` are old-valid/new-invalid. R6 reference-only and concept-only reasons can be transformed to R4 arrays; combined CodeableReference entries are not cleanly R4-representable because R4 has no per-entry pairing container.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Convert R4 `reasonCode` entries to `reason[].concept` and `reasonReference` entries to `reason[].reference`. For R6-to-R4, preserve combined concept/reference pairs with extensions or mapping metadata if the association is meaningful.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The unified representation is justified by better modeling of coded/linked reasons, especially with the new `doNotPerform` semantic. A less disruptive design would have kept the old arrays as aliases, but that would weaken the single-source R6 representation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 separated coded and referenced reasons into `reasonCode` and `reasonReference`; R6 merges them into repeatable `reason` CodeableReference. This is a real wire and generated-model break, and R6-to-R4 conversion can lose the pairing of a concept with a reference. The R6 design is nevertheless coherent because the merged container directly represents one reason that may be coded, referenced, or both. Keeping old arrays as aliases would preserve old data but create competing same-resource representations.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `reasonCode` is 0..* CodeableConcept with condition-code example binding.
R4 StructureDefinition: `reasonReference` is 0..* Reference(Condition|Observation|DiagnosticReport|DocumentReference).
R6 StructureDefinition: `reason` is 0..* CodeableReference with the same reference targets and condition-code example binding.
R6 `reason` comment ties reasons to `doNotPerform` when the request is negative.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use softens the stability concern, but reason information can be medically and reimbursement relevant. The judgment is softened from design revisit because the R6 CodeableReference merge has a strong modeling rationale and the main forward mapping is straightforward.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 reason arrays are not R6 fields; reverse conversion of combined CodeableReference entries can be lossy because R4 lacks a per-reason pairing container.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. Deprecated `reasonCode` and `reasonReference` aliases could preserve R4 instances, but they would duplicate `reason` and cannot cleanly represent one R6 reason containing both concept and reference without extra pairing metadata.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact and partial-alternative judgment: the break is material, but I judge it proportionate rather than a revisit item.

findings.title: doNotPerform was added as a modifier that can negate the request

oldState.summary: R4 had no local DeviceRequest element for a negative request to stop or not start using a device.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 DeviceRequest represented positive requests only in the base element set; any negative-order semantics would need profiles, status, reason text, or extensions.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional doNotPerform boolean, 0..1, isModifier true, summary true.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labeled as a modifier because this element negates the request to occur (ie, this is a request for the medication not to be ordered or prescribed, etc.)

semanticText.short: True if the request is to stop or not to start using the device
semanticText.definition: If true, indicates that the provider is asking for the patient to either stop using or to not start using the specified device or category of devices.
semanticText.comment: If do not perform is not specified, the request is a positive request e.g. "do perform".

newState.narrativeMd: `doNotPerform=true` reverses the clinical meaning from an order to provide/use a device to an order not to provide/use it.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Adding an optional element does not invalidate R4 data moving forward, but this is a modifier. If an R6 negative request is down-converted to R4 or consumed by software that ignores the new modifier, the meaning can invert from "do not use/provide" to "use/provide".
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: A dropped negation can create direct patient-safety risk, such as providing a device the clinician explicitly ordered the patient not to use.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Explicit support for negative DeviceRequests is a reasonable and safety-relevant R6 goal, and making the element a modifier is appropriate because it can invert the request. This is not an old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 base-design break: R4 instances remain valid when moving forward. The compatibility concern is that R6 negative requests cannot be safely down-converted or consumed by systems that ignore the modifier.
justification.inferredGoal: Support explicit negative DeviceRequests such as stopping or not starting a device.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 alternative is needed; this optional R6 modifier does not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Using an extension or profile to carry negation would be a backport or migration mitigation, not a less-breaking R6 base design for preserving R4 instances. Because the R6 field is optional and additive, `backwardCompatibleAlternativeAvailable` is best calibrated as Not applicable.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The material risk is R6-to-R4 conversion: negation must be preserved or rejected, but extension backports are mitigations rather than base-design alternatives.

evidence.detail: R6 defines doNotPerform as 0..1 boolean, isModifier true, isSummary true.
The definition says true means the provider asks the patient to stop using or not start using the device.
R4 has no DeviceRequest.doNotPerform element.

examples.examplesMd: Dropping `doNotPerform` from the R6 example would make the request look like an ordinary positive order for contact lenses.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 introduces `doNotPerform` as a local modifier on DeviceRequest. This is not an R4-to-R6 validation break, but it is one of the most important runtime risks because consumers must notice and honor it before acting on the request.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R6 instances with `doNotPerform=true` are not faithfully representable in base R4 DeviceRequest. Validation alone may not catch semantic loss if a converter simply drops unknown R6 fields. Runtime consumers that ignore modifiers can invert the order.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: R6-aware consumers must include `doNotPerform` in modifier handling, summaries, decision support, and fulfillment logic. R6-to-R4 conversion should use an explicit extension or reject/downscope negative requests unless a safe receiving-system agreement exists.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A modifier extension would have been more wire-compatible but less safe because many clients ignore unfamiliar extensions. A base modifier element is clinically clearer, so the breaking/round-trip risk is probably justified.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `doNotPerform` is an additive R6 modifier, so it does not make R4 instances invalid when moving forward. The compatibility concern is semantic and reverse-direction: dropping or ignoring `doNotPerform=true` can invert a request from `do not provide/use this device` into an apparent positive order. Making this a base modifier is a proportionate safety design because an extension-only approach would be easier to ignore.
keyEvidence: R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.doNotPerform` is 0..1 boolean, isModifier true, and isSummary true.
R6 definition: true means the provider asks the patient to stop using or not start using the specified device or device category.
R4 StructureDefinition: no `DeviceRequest.doNotPerform` element is present.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use lowers the general compatibility burden, but this modifier has clear patient-safety semantics. Low FMM does not justify ignoring a negation flag.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 negative requests cannot be faithfully represented in base R4 without an extension or rejection policy, and runtime consumers that ignore the modifier may act on the opposite meaning.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable as a forward-compatibility alternative. The R6 element is optional and does not invalidate R4 instances; R4 extensions are useful mitigations for down-conversion but are not less-breaking R6 base designs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing impact direction and not-applicable alternative judgment: this is high-risk if ignored, but the additive modifier is justified.

findings.title: R6 adds quantity and location details with no native R4 DeviceRequest fields

oldState.summary: R4 DeviceRequest had no direct quantity or preferred device-use location elements.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could sometimes approximate details through `parameter`, `subject`, `encounter`, notes, or extensions, but there was no native `quantity` or `location` slot.

newState.summary: R6 adds quantity 0..1 integer and location 0..* CodeableReference(Location).

binding.description: A location type where devices are delivered.

semanticText.definition: The number of devices to be provided; the preferred location(s) where the device should actually be used.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 can express how many devices are to be provided and where the device should be used, including coded/free-text or Location references.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not break R4 data validating as R6. The risk is reverse conversion and older runtime code: R6 can carry quantity/location semantics that base R4 cannot represent without extensions or lossy notes/parameters.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Quantity and use location can affect supply, reimbursement, delivery, and safe use.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding explicit quantity and location elements is a reasonable R6 expressiveness improvement and does not make any R4-valid DeviceRequest invalid in R6. The reported compatibility issue is R6-to-R4 representability, not R4-to-R6 base breakage. Under the calibration rules, ordinary extension backports for R4 systems should not be counted as a Yes or Partial base-design alternative.
justification.inferredGoal: Represent supply quantity and preferred use/delivery location explicitly.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable because optional R6 quantity and location fields preserve all R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The relevant compatibility path is conversion policy: preserve R6 `quantity` and `location` in extensions, a profile convention, or reject lossy down-conversion. Those choices do not indicate a less-breaking R6 base design was available because the R6 additions are forward-compatible for R4 data.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 receivers need extension or profile policy for down-conversion; that is a mitigation for new R6 content, not a less-breaking R6 base design.

evidence.detail: R6 adds quantity as 0..1 integer.
R6 adds location as 0..* CodeableReference(Location) with an example ServiceDeliveryLocationRoleType binding.
R4 has no DeviceRequest.quantity or DeviceRequest.location element.

examples.examplesMd: R4 conversion would need an extension, a parameter convention, or a note; none is a native semantic equivalent.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds explicit quantity and location elements. These are useful and optional, but they introduce R6 content that cannot be faithfully carried by an R4 DeviceRequest without an agreed extension or profile convention.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation is not broken by these additions. R6-to-R4 conversion is potentially lossy because base R4 has no `quantity` or `location` fields; strict R4 validators will reject unknown direct elements.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For down-conversion, map these values to named cross-version extensions or a profile-specific `parameter` convention only when all parties agree. Test quantity zero/positive edge cases according to local profiles, and test both coded and referenced locations.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Because the elements are optional, adding them is a normal forward-compatible evolution for R6. The unavoidable backward-compatibility issue is that R4 receivers need an extension or must reject/ignore the new data.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds optional `quantity` and `location` fields. These additions increase expressiveness but do not reject any R4 DeviceRequest instance. Older R4 receivers need a down-conversion policy if R6 data uses these fields, yet that is the normal cost of new optional content rather than a base R4-to-R6 compatibility design problem.
keyEvidence: R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.quantity` is 0..1 integer.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.location` is 0..* CodeableReference(Location) with an example location-type binding.
R4 StructureDefinition: no direct `DeviceRequest.quantity` or `DeviceRequest.location` element is present.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use further reduces concern. Quantity and location can matter operationally, but the change is additive and optional.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: new R6 quantity/location values need extensions, profiles, or rejection when sent to R4 systems; there is no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable. Avoiding the fields or using only extensions would reduce R6 expressiveness and is not needed to preserve R4-valid instances.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and alternative judgment: the reverse representability issue is real, but I would classify the additive optional change as no standards-design problem.

findings.title: R6 adds asNeeded and asNeededFor to represent PRN device use

oldState.summary: R4 had no native PRN/as-needed DeviceRequest fields.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could imply PRN behavior through occurrence Timing text, notes, reasons, parameters, or extensions, but not with dedicated base elements.

newState.summary: R6 adds asNeeded 0..1 boolean and asNeededFor 0..1 CodeableConcept.

semanticText.definition: PRN status of request and the reason for using the device.

newState.narrativeMd: `asNeeded` marks PRN use and `asNeededFor` states the reason for that use.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The additions are optional, so they do not invalidate R4 data moving forward. They do introduce R6 PRN semantics that older R4 receivers may ignore or lose, which can change scheduling and use instructions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: PRN device-use conditions can be clinically important for when a patient should use equipment.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Dedicated PRN fields are a reasonable R6 goal because they reduce ambiguity in device-use instructions. Since these elements are optional additions, there is no R4-to-R6 base instance break to avoid. The compatibility risk lies in older R4 systems losing new R6 PRN semantics during down-conversion.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable because optional R6 asNeeded and asNeededFor fields do not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Relying on `occurrence[x]`, notes, or extensions for PRN semantics would avoid new R6 content but would also keep the ambiguity R6 is trying to remove. For calibration, those are R4 backport or migration strategies, not evidence of a less-breaking base R6 alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R4 extension or Timing-note conventions are down-conversion mitigations, not backward-compatible R6 base-design alternatives.

evidence.detail: R6 adds asNeeded as 0..1 boolean.
R6 adds asNeededFor as 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R4 has no DeviceRequest.asNeeded or DeviceRequest.asNeededFor element.

examples.examplesMd: An R4 representation would need a profile convention, such as an extension or a Timing/notes convention, and may not round-trip cleanly.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 can now say a device is to be used as needed and record the reason. R4 has no corresponding base fields, so down-conversion can lose instructions that affect patient behavior.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No old-valid/new-invalid issue exists for R4-to-R6. R6 instances using these elements are not base-R4 representable without extensions, and R4 consumers that ignore the information may treat a conditional request as routine or scheduled.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4, define explicit extensions for `asNeeded` and `asNeededFor` or reject the conversion if PRN semantics are safety-relevant. Include tests where `asNeeded=false`, `asNeeded=true` without reason, and `asNeeded=true` with reason appear.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The optional addition is reasonable and less disruptive than changing existing occurrence semantics. The compatibility burden belongs in cross-version extensions and receiver capability checks.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds optional PRN fields, `asNeeded` and `asNeededFor`. This does not invalidate old R4 instances; it only creates new R6 content that R4 systems cannot natively carry. Because the fields are optional and directly improve clarity of device-use instructions, the compatibility burden belongs in down-conversion policy rather than standards redesign.
keyEvidence: R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.asNeeded` is 0..1 boolean.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.asNeededFor` is 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R4 StructureDefinition: no `DeviceRequest.asNeeded` or `DeviceRequest.asNeededFor` element is present.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use softens concern. PRN semantics can be clinically meaningful, but there is no forward R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 PRN values require extensions, narrative, profile conventions, or rejection when converted to R4; old R4 data remains valid with respect to this addition.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable. Keeping PRN semantics only in timing, notes, or extensions would avoid new R6 content but would not preserve an old base field, because none existed in R4.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and not-applicable alternative judgment: the migration note is useful, but the additive optional fields are not a material R4-to-R6 problem.

findings.title: requester reference targets were widened to CareTeam, Group, Patient, and RelatedPerson

oldState.summary: R4 requester allowed Device, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, or Organization.

semanticText.definition: The individual who initiated the request and has responsibility for its activation.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 requester was limited to devices and professional/organizational requesters.

newState.summary: R6 requester also allows CareTeam, Group, Patient, and RelatedPerson.

semanticText.definition: The individual or entity who initiated the request and has responsibility for its activation.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 supports broader submitter categories, including patient and related-person requesters.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Widening a target list does not invalidate R4 instances in R6. It does allow R6 instances that R4 validators and generated reference-type unions may reject.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Requester identity affects authorization, provenance, and workflow routing, but the added targets are usually representable only with policy decisions in R4.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Supporting patient, related-person, group, and care-team requesters is a reasonable R6 workflow expansion. Because all R4 requester target profiles remain allowed, the base change is forward-compatible for R4 instances. The remaining issue is R6-to-R4 target representability and generated-code updates, so the backward-compatible alternative field should be Not applicable rather than Partial.
justification.inferredGoal: Support a broader set of request submitters, including patient-initiated and team/group requests.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable; widening requester targets preserves all R4 requester references.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A profile-only widening could have limited base R6 change, but it would not be a backward-compatible alternative to an R4-to-R6 break because no such forward break exists. Down-conversion still needs policy for the added target types.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Older R4 validators may reject new R6 requester target types, but no less-breaking alternative is needed for R4-to-R6 compatibility.

evidence.detail: R4 requester targets Device, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, and Organization.
R6 adds CareTeam, Group, Patient, and RelatedPerson to requester targets.

examples.examplesMd: A Patient requester is valid against the R6 target list but not against the R4 DeviceRequest requester target list.

findings.narrativeMd: `requester` is wider in R6. This is mostly a reverse-compatibility and generated-code risk: R4 target-type checks may reject R6 requesters that are clinically valid in R6.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation remains safe because all R4 targets are still allowed. R6-to-R4 conversion must handle the four added target types explicitly; otherwise strict R4 validation fails.

findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is a low-disruption forward-compatible widening, but it still affects older validators. A profile-only widening would protect base R4 compatibility but fragment behavior across implementations.

R4 validators and generated unions may reject new R6 requester types, but that is a reverse-compatibility concern caused by added expressiveness.

findings.title: status required binding adds the ended code in R6

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: No expansion service was used; codes were compared from the local CodeSystem resources included in the core packages.

oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 request-status CodeSystem did not contain `ended`.

findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update R6 enum handling to include `ended`. For down-conversion, use an official ConceptMap if available or require human/business policy to choose between extension preservation, rejection, or local mapping.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The code addition is semantically useful but not backward-compatible for required-binding consumers. A less disruptive approach would have used existing statuses plus reason/detail, but that sacrifices precision.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `status` keeps its shape and required binding but the R6 request-status code system includes `ended`. No R4 status code is removed, so R4 data remains valid going forward. The compatibility burden is reverse-direction and runtime enum handling: an R4 system receiving `ended` cannot validate or interpret it without a mapping policy. Since `status` controls whether a request should be acted upon, this is real migration work, but the new code fills a plausible workflow gap.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 tightens lifecycle expectations for updates to the same DeviceRequest instance.

facts.newValue: This element is immutable. It cannot be changed for the same resource instance.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a single-instance validation break in the StructureDefinition, but it affects update semantics and conformance. Systems that allowed an existing DeviceRequest to move from proposal to order, for example, may need to create a replacement resource instead.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Intent changes can affect authorization and audit semantics; immutability helps prevent reinterpretation of historical records.

justification.justificationRationaleMd: Preventing in-place changes to `intent` is a reasonable goal because intent modifies interpretation and affects auditability. A less-breaking approach could have introduced warning-level guidance first, but that would leave inconsistent lifecycle behavior across implementations. Since the change is semantic rather than a single-instance validation break, and the softer path only partially meets the audit-safety goal, the R6 choice is probably justified.
justification.inferredGoal: Prevent a resource instance from changing workflow class after creation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Make intent immutability a best-practice warning or profile/lifecycle rule rather than base conformance text.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best alternative would express immutability as best-practice guidance, a warning invariant, or a profile rule for stricter workflows. That would reduce disruption for systems that promoted a request by updating `intent`, but it would not give base R6 consumers the same consistent guarantee about resource lifecycle semantics.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Softer guidance preserves more existing update workflows but weakens audit consistency for a modifier element that changes request meaning.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds an explicit immutability rule for `intent`. Even without a new invariant in the snapshot, this is a conformance-text change that can affect servers, audit policies, and client update workflows.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A standalone R4 instance does not become invalid solely because of this text. The risk appears when comparing versions of the same resource instance or enforcing update rules: changing intent in-place is no longer conformant under the R6 comment.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review workflows that promote, clone, or revise DeviceRequests by changing `intent`. Prefer creating a new resource with appropriate relationship links rather than mutating the original intent. Add tests for update/patch logic if the system enforces immutability.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The rule is defensible because `intent` changes the interpretation of the resource. A backward-compatible option would have been warning-level guidance, but that would allow inconsistent lifecycle behavior.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 adds conformance text that `intent` is immutable for the same resource instance. A single R4 instance is not invalidated, but update workflows that promoted one resource from proposal to order by changing `intent` now conflict with the R6 lifecycle expectation. The rule is proportionate because `intent` is a modifier that changes how all descriptive fields are interpreted; softer guidance would be less disruptive but would not give receivers a stable lifecycle guarantee.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.intent` has no inspected immutability comment.
R6 StructureDefinition: `DeviceRequest.intent.comment` says `This element is immutable. It cannot be changed for the same resource instance.`
`intent` is 1..1, required-bound, isModifier, and isSummary in both R4 and R6.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Supplied R4 FMM 1/trial-use softens the concern, especially because this is prose rather than a new invariant. The remaining concern is limited to systems with same-resource intent mutation workflows.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: the instance wire shape is unchanged, but server update policy, audit logic, and conformance checks may need to treat intent changes as invalid lifecycle transitions.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have introduced this as best-practice guidance, warning-level policy, or profile guidance first, but that would weaken the computable and audit expectation for a modifier element.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing impact and partial-alternative judgment: the update-semantics risk is real, but low FMM and lack of a formal invariant keep it proportionate.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: The R6 StructureDefinition is present with the same canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, baseDefinition, derivation, and non-abstract flag as R4. Status changed from draft to active but this is not an instance-shape break.

Material type changes are covered in findings. Checked unchanged local type domains include `occurrence[x]` (dateTime/Period/Timing), `parameter.value[x]` (CodeableConcept/Quantity/Range/boolean), `subject`, `encounter`, `insurance`, `supportingInfo`, `note`, `relevantHistory`, `basedOn`, `identifier`, and `groupIdentifier`.

Reference target changes for `replaces`, `product[x]`, `performer`, `reason`, `location`, and `requester` are covered in findings. `subject` remained Patient/Group/Location/Device in the inspected R4 and R6 snapshots; `basedOn`, `encounter`, `insurance`, `supportingInfo`, and `relevantHistory` showed no material local target change.

`priority` required binding retained the same local request-priority codes. `status` and `intent` required-binding additions are findings. `product[x]` and `parameter.code` example-binding changes are not hard validation breaks.
No local DeviceRequest-specific invariants were added or removed beyond inherited Element/DomainResource/Extension constraint text changes, which are out of scope.
No fixed, pattern, or default value constraints were identified on local DeviceRequest elements in the compared snapshots.
No maxLength, minValue, maxValue, or regex changes were identified for local DeviceRequest elements.
Existing local `status` and `intent` modifier flags remained modifiers. The new local `doNotPerform` modifier is a finding. Inherited modifierExtension/base flag changes are out of scope.
Material local summary-flag effects are associated with added/removed elements in findings. The observed `modifierExtension` summary change is inherited/base content and excluded.
No slicing changes were identified for local DeviceRequest elements.
Material local semantic text changes are captured for `performer`, `reason`, `doNotPerform`, and `intent`. Minor wording updates elsewhere did not appear to change validation or migration behavior.
The resource type and canonical identity did not change. Serialization-breaking local changes are the element renames and CodeableReference representation changes captured in findings.
R6-to-R4 risks were assessed for new elements, added reference targets, new required-binding codes, `productCanonical`, and CodeableReference pairings. Official ConceptMaps would improve confidence.
